title: Increasing or decreasing
text: A "one-to-one" function must assign a unique output to every unique input. On the interval $$[\pi/4,3\pi/4],$$ what happens to $$\sin(x)$$ as you move away from $$x=\frac{\pi}{2}$$ toward either endpoint? What does this imply about output values?
choices: $$\sin(x)$$ decreases toward both $$x=\frac{\pi}{4}$$ and $$x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$$, so $$\sin(x)$$ fails the horizontal line test as there is a peak at $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$
$$\sin(x)$$ increases toward both $$x=\frac{\pi}{4}$$ and $$x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$$, so $$\sin(x)$$ fails the horizontal line test as there is a valley at $$x=\frac{\pi}{2}$$
\n$$\sin(x)$$ decreases toward $$x=\frac{\pi}{4}$$ and increases toward $$x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$$, so outputs are all unique
$$\sin(x)$$ increases toward $$x=\frac{\pi}{4}$$ and decreases toward $$x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$$, so outputs are all unique

title: Test midpoints and end points
text: Calculate $$\sin(\pi/3)$$ and $$\sin(2\pi/3).$$ If these values are identical, the function has "doubled back" on itself.

title: Graph the function
text: Visualize the graph. The function increases from $$x=\frac{\pi}{4}$$ up to $$x=\frac{\pi}{2}$$, then decreases to $$x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$$, meaning it doubles back through the same output values.\n##figure1.gif##
